title: Networks: VPC, subnets and endpoints

story: A poisoned Jira comment tells Nova to upload the fcp repo to a paste site, and Nova tries. The first attempt goes through the egress proxy, the one server that may talk to the internet for the VMs, and the proxy refuses it because the site is not on its short list (a later lesson builds that proxy). So Nova tries again with a script that connects to the site directly. This time nothing refuses anything. The command waits, and after a while it fails with a timeout. Nobody wrote a rule about paste sites, and no log line says "blocked". The packets simply had nowhere to go, because the network Nova's VM sits on has no road to the internet at all.

Yet the same VM is not cut off from everything. A minute earlier it received its task through AWS Systems Manager, and later it will save its notes to an S3 bucket. Both of those are AWS services that normally live at public internet addresses.
hook.question: How do you build a network where a machine cannot reach the internet, but can still reach the few AWS services it needs?

read.h: Your own network, with your own addresses
p: A VPC, a virtual private cloud, is a private network inside your AWS account. Machines you start get addresses from its range, and nothing reaches them or leaves them unless you build the path. You write the range as a CIDR block: a start address, a slash and a number that says how many of the first bits are fixed. In 10.60.0.0/16 the first 16 bits (10.60) are fixed and the other 16 are free, so the block holds every address from 10.60.0.0 to 10.60.255.255, 65,536 in all. A bigger number after the slash means a smaller block: a /18 holds 16,384 addresses and a /28 holds only 16.

A VPC is cut into subnets, smaller blocks that each live in one availability zone. The sandbox VPC uses 10.60.0.0/16, a range no other network of ours uses, and splits it into four /18 blocks: three for VMs, one in each zone, and the fourth kept for the egress proxy that a later lesson builds. OpenTofu, the tool our infrastructure code is written in, has a function that does the cutting, and you can try it with no cloud at all.

code.text:
echo '[for n in range(3) : cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, n)]' | tofu console
echo 'cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, 3)' | tofu console

notes.text: cidrsubnet(range, extra bits, number): 2 extra bits turn a /16 into four /18 blocks, numbered 0 to 3. These are the three VM subnets.
Block number 3, the spare one for the proxy.

read.h: The route table decides where packets can go
p: Before the AWS version, look at one you already have. Every container on your laptop has a route table, and you can print it. The first container below is on Docker's normal network, the second on a network created with --internal.

code.text:
docker run --rm alpine:3.20 sh -c 'ip route; wget -q -T 3 --spider http://1.1.1.1 && echo "1.1.1.1 is reachable"'

docker network create --internal sandbox-net
docker run --rm --network sandbox-net alpine:3.20 sh -c 'ip route; wget -q -T 3 --spider http://1.1.1.1 && echo "1.1.1.1 is reachable"'

notes.text: ip route prints the container's route table; wget tries to reach a public address.
--internal creates a network with no route out of your laptop.

read.see:
default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0
172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 scope link  src 172.17.0.5
1.1.1.1 is reachable

172.21.0.0/16 dev eth0 scope link  src 172.21.0.2
wget: can't connect to remote host (1.1.1.1): Network unreachable

deeper.h: Go deeper: security groups, a firewall on each machine
p: Routes say where a packet can go. A security group says which connections a machine accepts and starts, and it is attached to the machine's network card. Ingress rules say what may come in, egress rules what may go out, and replies to an allowed connection always get back. Security groups have no deny rules: you block something by not allowing it, and a new group allows all egress until you remove that rule.

The sandbox security group has no ingress rules at all, so nobody can connect to a sandbox. Its egress rules allow only three destinations: the egress proxy on port 3128, the endpoints on port 443, and the private path to our own services. Routes and security groups are two separate walls, and each one would stop the paste-site upload by itself.

read.h: No default route, no way out
p: The difference between the two outputs is one line. The first table has a default route, a catch-all for every address that matches nothing more specific, and it sends that traffic to a gateway that leads to the internet. The second table knows only its own block, so a packet for 1.1.1.1 matches no route, and the container gives up at once with "Network unreachable".

In a VPC every subnet has a route table that works the same way, with one row per destination and target. A new VPC starts with a single route: its own range goes to local, which means the machines inside can reach each other. A public subnet adds a default route, written 0.0.0.0/0, to an internet gateway, the VPC's door to the internet. A typical private subnet adds 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway instead, which lets machines call out without anyone calling in. The sandbox subnets get neither, so their only route is local.

Here the Docker example stops matching. On a VM, the operating system sends every outside packet to the VPC's router, and the subnet's route table is applied there, inside the AWS network. With no matching route, AWS drops the packet without a word, so the VM sees a timeout instead of "Network unreachable", as in the story. And because that table lives in AWS, even root on the VM cannot add a road the subnet does not have.

read.h: Endpoints: private doors to AWS services
p: A VM with only a local route still needs a few AWS services. The SSM agent on it must receive commands from AWS Systems Manager, Docker must pull images from ECR, and the run's notes go to S3. Those services answer at public addresses, so without help the VM could not reach them either. A VPC endpoint is a private path from your VPC to one AWS service, and it comes in two kinds.

An interface endpoint is a network card with a private address in each of your subnets. With private DNS turned on, a name like ssm.us-east-1.amazonaws.com resolves inside the VPC to that private address, so the SSM agent connects to it without any route to the internet. A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB. Instead of a network card, it adds a route to the route table whose destination is a prefix list, an AWS-managed list of S3's address ranges, so S3 traffic stays inside AWS. Gateway endpoints are free; interface endpoints cost a small amount per hour.

An endpoint has its own policy, a third check after the route table and the security group (the firewall on each machine, explained in a panel above). If the S3 endpoint allowed every bucket, a fooled agent could upload our code to a bucket that belongs to somebody else, through a link that person gave it, and the traffic would look like ordinary S3. So the sandbox's S3 endpoint allows only our own buckets. Once the endpoint exists, the route table gets one new line, shown below the policy: S3's prefix list (pl-…) now goes to the endpoint (vpce-…).

code.file: s3-endpoint-policy.json (the policy of the S3 gateway endpoint)

notes.text: Principal "*": the endpoint does not care who calls; IAM still checks the caller afterwards.
Only objects in our runs bucket. Any other bucket, even one with a valid link, is refused at the endpoint.

deeper.h: Go deeper: DNS, the last quiet way out
p: Even with no route out, a VM can still ask the VPC's DNS resolver for a name, and the resolver asks the internet on the VM's behalf. An attacker who owns a domain can read every lookup for it, so a lookup for c2VjcmV0.attacker.example carries data inside the name itself. This is called DNS exfiltration.

The sandbox VPC closes it with a DNS firewall, a Route 53 Resolver feature. One list holds the names the VMs may look up: the proxy's allow-list, *.amazonaws.com and our own service names. An ALLOW rule lets those through, and a BLOCK rule answers NXDOMAIN, "no such name", for everything else.

lab.title: A network with no way out
needs: AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab
OpenTofu (brew install opentofu), only for tofu console
lab.goal: Build the sandbox VPC on a practice AWS, prove its only route is local, and add private doors to S3 and Systems Manager without opening a road to the internet.

guess.q: A subnet's route table has one route: 10.60.0.0/16 to local. A VM in that subnet runs curl https://example.com. What happens?

options.text: A firewall blocks the request and writes it to a log.
options.why: No firewall is needed. The packet matches no route, so it never leaves the subnet.

options.text: The request fails, because no route matches the address.
options.why: Private in AWS means no route out. Only addresses inside 10.60.0.0/16, and any endpoints you add, have a path.

options.text: It works, because AWS gives every VPC a path to the internet by default.
options.why: A new VPC has only the local route. A path out exists only if someone adds an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.

follow.say: Feel the idea on your laptop first: one container with a default route and one without.
follow.do:
docker run --rm alpine:3.20 sh -c 'ip route; wget -q -T 3 --spider http://1.1.1.1 && echo "1.1.1.1 is reachable"'
docker network create --internal sandbox-net
docker run --rm --network sandbox-net alpine:3.20 sh -c 'ip route; wget -q -T 3 --spider http://1.1.1.1 && echo "1.1.1.1 is reachable"'
follow.see:
default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0
172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 scope link  src 172.17.0.5
1.1.1.1 is reachable
(the network ID)
172.21.0.0/16 dev eth0 scope link  src 172.21.0.2
wget: can't connect to remote host (1.1.1.1): Network unreachable

follow.say: Plan the addresses before you create anything, because subnets cannot be resized later.
follow.do: echo '[for n in range(3) : cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, n)]' | tofu console

follow.say: Start LocalStack again (skip the first line if it is still running from p3-1), and point the AWS CLI at it in this terminal.
follow.do:
docker run --rm -d --name localstack -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
follow.see: (a container ID, then nothing: the export prints no output)

follow.say: Create the VPC and one subnet per availability zone. Keep this terminal open, because $VPC is used in every later step.
follow.do:
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.60.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text) && echo $VPC
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.60.0.0/18 --availability-zone us-east-1a --query 'Subnet.[CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]' --output text
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.60.64.0/18 --availability-zone us-east-1b --query 'Subnet.[CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]' --output text
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.60.128.0/18 --availability-zone us-east-1c --query 'Subnet.[CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]' --output text
follow.see:
vpc-8d31a58a977d3ad69
10.60.0.0/18	us-east-1a
10.60.64.0/18	us-east-1b
10.60.128.0/18	us-east-1c
(your VPC ID is different)

follow.say: Read the routes, and count the doors to the internet, because "no way out" should be something you can check, not something you believe.
follow.do:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock || DestinationPrefixListId, GatewayId]' --output text
echo "internet gateways: $(aws ec2 describe-internet-gateways --filters Name=attachment.vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'length(InternetGateways)'), NAT gateways: $(aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'length(NatGateways)')"

follow.say: Add the S3 gateway endpoint with a policy that allows only the runs bucket, and see the route it adds.
follow.do:
Save the endpoint policy from Understand as s3-endpoint-policy.json, then:
RT=$(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'RouteTables[0].RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 --route-table-ids $RT --policy-document file://s3-endpoint-policy.json --query 'VpcEndpoint.[VpcEndpointType,State]' --output text
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock || DestinationPrefixListId, GatewayId]' --output text
follow.see:
Gateway	available
10.60.0.0/16	local
pl-5b445bd3f7bc20506	vpce-c9e6f205668944939
(the pl- line is the new route: S3's address list goes to the endpoint, not to the internet)

lab.build: The SSM agent on the VM needs three interface endpoints: ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages (the service names are com.amazonaws.us-east-1.<name>). Create all three in the three subnets with private DNS turned on; you can get the subnet IDs with aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'Subnets[].SubnetId' --output text. Then write one describe-vpc-endpoints command that prints the type, the service name and the number of network cards of every endpoint in $VPC. Last, read the routes again: did the interface endpoints add any route?
checks: The first container prints a default route and reaches 1.1.1.1; the one on sandbox-net has no default route and prints Network unreachable.
Your VPC has three /18 subnets in us-east-1a, b and c.
Before the endpoint, the route table has only 10.60.0.0/16 to local, with 0 internet gateways and 0 NAT gateways.
After the S3 endpoint, there is one extra route from a pl- prefix list to a vpce- endpoint.
describe-vpc-endpoints prints one Gateway line and three Interface lines, each Interface endpoint with 3 network cards, and the route table did not change.
You stopped LocalStack (docker stop localstack) and removed the Docker network (docker network rm sandbox-net).

solution.text:
for svc in ssm ssmmessages ec2messages; do
  aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
    --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.$svc --private-dns-enabled \
    --subnet-ids $(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'Subnets[].SubnetId' --output text) \
    --query 'VpcEndpoint.ServiceName' --output text
done

aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC \
  --query 'VpcEndpoints[].[VpcEndpointType,ServiceName,length(NetworkInterfaceIds)]' --output text
# Gateway    com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3           0
# Interface  com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ssm          3
# Interface  com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ssmmessages  3
# Interface  com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ec2messages  3
# The routes are unchanged: interface endpoints are reached through the local route.

lab.fix: A teammate copied the network from the product's VPC module, which builds public subnets, and "fixed" a slow npm install by adding a road out. Recreate their change: IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text), then aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id $IGW --vpc-id $VPC, then aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $RT --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW. Read the routes and find the line that breaks the wall. Remove it with delete-route, then detach and delete the internet gateway, and prove with your two checking commands that the VPC is back to local plus the S3 route, with 0 internet gateways.
explain: Why does a curl to a paste site fail on a sandbox VM even though no rule mentions paste sites?
What is the difference between a gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint, and why does only one of them change the route table?
Why does the S3 endpoint list our bucket, when S3 is an AWS service and not the open internet?
lab.done: Your VPC has three subnets, only the local route plus the S3 endpoint route, one gateway and three interface endpoints, and no internet gateway.

check.q: A sandbox subnet's route table has 10.60.0.0/16 to local and an S3 prefix list to an endpoint. A fooled agent sends the repo to a paste site. What stops it first?

options.text: The packet matches no route, so it never leaves the subnet
options.why: There is no default route and no internet gateway or NAT gateway. AWS drops the packets and the request times out, before any firewall is involved.

options.text: The S3 endpoint policy refuses the upload
options.why: The endpoint policy only sees traffic that goes to S3. A paste site is not S3, so the packet never reaches the endpoint.

options.text: The IAM role of the VM has no permission for the paste site
options.why: IAM only checks calls to AWS APIs. It has nothing to say about a request to some other website.

check.q: Why does the sandbox VM need interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages?

options.text: So people can connect to the VM over SSH through the endpoint
options.why: Endpoints let the VM reach an AWS service. They open no way for anyone to connect to the VM.

options.text: Because without them the VM cannot start
options.why: The VM starts fine. It would only be unreachable for Systems Manager, so no one could send it commands.

options.text: So the SSM agent can reach Systems Manager with private addresses, without any route to the internet
options.why: With private DNS on, the service names resolve to network cards inside the subnets, which the local route already covers.

check.q: A teammate wants the S3 endpoint policy to allow every bucket, because "it is only S3 after all". What is the risk?

options.why: An open policy reaches our bucket too. The problem is everything else it also reaches.

options.text: A fooled agent could upload our code to someone else's bucket with a link they provide
options.why: S3 is a service anyone can have a bucket in. Listing only our buckets closes that quiet way out.

options.text: Gateway endpoints become expensive with an open policy
options.why: Gateway endpoints cost nothing either way. The reason is safety, not money.

p: The sandbox network is a private-only copy of our usual VPC module, built in the ai-agents account with the range 10.60.0.0/16: three /18 subnets, no internet gateway, no NAT, no public addresses, flow logs always on, an S3 gateway endpoint limited to our buckets and the interface endpoints a sandbox needs. A DNS firewall and a private DNS zone for our service names come with it, and the account's SCPs stop anyone from adding a NAT gateway or a peering later.

The only machines in the account with a route to the internet are the two egress proxy servers, in their own small subnets cut from the spare /18. The sandbox security group lets a VM reach the proxy, the endpoints and the private path to the broker, the gateway and the telemetry collector, and nothing else.

tickets.why: The private-only VPC module: three /18 subnets, no internet gateway or NAT, a narrow S3 endpoint and interface endpoints.
Builds the sandbox VPC on 10.60.0.0/16 with the DNS firewall, the private zone and the runs bucket.
The sandbox security group: no ingress, egress only to the proxy, the endpoints and the private path.
The proxy subnets: the only route to the internet in the account.

words.plain: Virtual private cloud: your own private network in an AWS account, with an address range you choose.
An address range written as start/size, like 10.60.0.0/16; a bigger number after the slash means fewer addresses.
A slice of the VPC's range in one availability zone, with its own route table.
The list of destination and target pairs that decides where packets from a subnet may go.
A private path from the VPC to one AWS service: a route (gateway) or a network card (interface).

review.q: Write the route table of a sandbox subnet from memory, and say which route an internet gateway would add.
review.a: 10.60.0.0/16 to local, plus S3's prefix list to the S3 gateway endpoint. An internet gateway would add 0.0.0.0/0 to igw-..., which the sandbox never gets.

review.q: Explain to a teammate why we use endpoints instead of a NAT gateway to reach SSM and S3.
review.a: A NAT gateway is a road to the whole internet. An endpoint reaches exactly one AWS service through private addresses, and the S3 one has a policy that limits it to our buckets.

review.q: How many addresses does a /18 hold, and why does the sandbox VPC have four of them?
review.a: 16,384. Three hold VMs, one per availability zone, and the fourth is kept for the egress proxy's own subnets.

remember: A machine can only send packets where its subnet's route table points, so a sandbox subnet has only the local route, and endpoints are the private doors to the AWS services it needs.
